title: TRISO-X, LLC; Special Nuclear Material License Application for the TRISO-X Fuel Fabrication Facility; Draft Environmental Impact Statement
summary:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission has released two major environmental reviews that could shape the next chapter of nuclear energy in America. First, it issued a final environmental review that supports granting a construction permit for TerraPower’s advanced reactor in Kemmerer, Wyoming. Second, it published a draft environmental review for a new nuclear fuel factory in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, and is asking for public comments through November 17, 2025.

In Wyoming, TerraPower’s project aims to build and operate a next‑generation reactor to replace power from retiring coal plants in the PacifiCorp service area. After weighing environmental effects alongside economic and technical factors, the regulator recommends moving forward with the construction permit unless safety issues emerge. The review did not find another option that better meets the project’s purpose with fewer environmental downsides.

In Tennessee, TRISO‑X is seeking a long‑term license to build and run a first‑of‑its‑kind facility to make advanced nuclear fuel. The draft review’s preliminary takeaway is similar: the regulator is inclined to issue the license, pending final safety and environmental findings. This decision is not final, and the public is invited to comment before the agency completes its analysis.

Who stands to benefit? Local communities could see new jobs, investment, and tax revenues. Utilities and customers may gain a steady, low‑carbon power source as coal plants retire. The broader energy sector could benefit from domestic fuel production and a more resilient grid.

Who might be negatively affected? Nearby residents could experience construction traffic, noise, and land disturbance, and will weigh ongoing safety and environmental risks, including waste handling and impacts on local ecosystems and historic sites. Workers and communities tied to legacy coal facilities may face uncertainty if transitions are uneven. There’s also the risk of cost overruns that could affect customers or taxpayers.

These reviews don’t end the conversation—they aim to inform it. If you live near these sites or work in energy, now is a good time to read the findings and, for the Tennessee fuel facility, share your views before the comment window closes.
